setup: Arms straight out in front at shoulder height, band taut but not stretched.
tempo: Pull over 1 second, hold the squeeze for 1, return over 2.
breathing: Out as you pull apart.
form_cues: Arms stay straight — bending them turns it into a row.
Squeeze the shoulder blades, do not just move the hands.
Use a light band; this is a warm-up, not a strength set.
why: The best 60-second insurance for a pressing session: it wakes up the rear delts and upper back that hold your shoulder in a good position under a bench or overhead press.
common_mistakes: A band so heavy the shoulders shrug up to move it.
Snapping it back instead of returning under control.

name: Open-Book Thoracic Rotation
instructions: Lie on your side with knees bent to 90° and both arms stretched out in front of you. Keeping your knees down, sweep the top arm in a wide arc across your body and open your chest toward the ceiling. Follow the hand with your eyes, then return.
setup: On your side, hips and knees at 90°, arms stacked straight out.
tempo: 6–8 per side, pausing 2 seconds at the open position.
breathing: Breathe out as you open, and use the exhale to get another inch.
form_cues: The knees stay pinned to the floor — if they lift, the rotation moved to the lower back.
Reach long through the fingertips rather than just dropping the arm.
Eyes track the hand; the head follows the chest.
why: Most people are stiff through the mid-back, which is what forces the lower back and shoulders to compensate on overhead work. This isolates rotation to the right segment.
common_mistakes: Letting the top knee lift, which moves the movement to the lumbar spine.
Forcing the arm to the floor rather than letting the chest open.

name: Standing Hamstring Stretch
instructions: Put one heel on a low step with your leg straight and toes pointing up. Keeping your back flat, hinge forward from the hips until you feel a stretch down the back of the thigh. Hold, then swap legs.
setup: One heel on a low box or step, standing leg soft, hands on the front thigh.
tempo: Hold 20–30 seconds per side, 2 rounds.
breathing: Slow breathing; let the muscle release on each exhale.
form_cues: Hinge at the hip with a flat back rather than rounding to reach further.
Point the toes of the raised foot up.
A firm stretch, never a sharp or nervy one.
why: The most useful post-training stretch for anyone who squats, hinges or sits at a desk. Holds of 20–30 seconds are enough — longer adds nothing for range.
common_mistakes: Rounding the back to touch the toes, which stretches the spine rather than the hamstring.
Doing this BEFORE lifting, where long static holds measurably reduce strength.

name: Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch
instructions: Kneel on one knee with the other foot flat in front. Squeeze the glute on the kneeling side and push your hips gently forward until you feel a stretch at the front of the hip. Stay tall. Hold, then swap.
setup: Half-kneeling, front shin vertical, back knee under or slightly behind the hip.
tempo: Hold 25–30 seconds per side, 2 rounds.
breathing: Breathe out slowly and let the hip settle forward.
form_cues: Squeeze the back glute FIRST — that is what actually lengthens the hip flexor.
Keep the ribs down; arching the lower back fakes the range.
Move the hips forward, do not lean the torso back.
why: Directly counteracts sitting, and tight hip flexors are one of the most common reasons people cannot finish a hip thrust or stand tall at the top of a deadlift.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back so the stretch is felt in the spine instead of the hip.
Leaning the torso backward rather than driving the hips forward.

name: Pigeon Stretch
instructions: From all fours, bring one shin forward across your body and slide the other leg straight back. Keep your hips square and lower your chest over the front shin as far as is comfortable. Hold, then swap.
setup: Front shin angled across the body, back leg straight behind, hips level.
tempo: Hold 30 seconds per side, breathing into it.
breathing: Deep and slow; sink a little further on each exhale.
form_cues: Keep the hips square — letting one side rise removes the stretch.
Put a cushion under the near hip if it does not reach the floor.
Stop well short of any pinching in the front of the hip or knee.
why: The most direct stretch there is for the glutes and deep hip rotators, which get short from heavy squatting and from sitting.
common_mistakes: Letting the hips rotate open so the stretch disappears.
Pushing into knee pain — the front knee should never be the thing you feel.

name: Child's Pose
instructions: Kneel, sit your hips back toward your heels and reach your arms long in front of you, letting your chest sink toward the floor. Rest your forehead down and breathe.
setup: Knees roughly hip-width or wider, big toes together, arms stretched forward.
tempo: Hold 30–60 seconds. This is the one you can stay in.
breathing: Slow deep breaths into the back of the ribs.
form_cues: Reach the hands away while the hips travel back — that is what lengthens the lats.
Widen the knees if your belly or hips block the position.
Let the shoulders relax rather than holding them up.
why: Decompresses the spine and lengthens the lats after pulling work, and it is the most reliable way to bring your breathing rate down at the end of a hard session.
common_mistakes: Keeping the shoulders active instead of letting the chest sink.
Knees too close together when the hips are tight, which blocks the position.

name: Doorway Chest Stretch
instructions: Stand in a doorway with your forearms on the frame, elbows at about shoulder height. Step one foot through and lean gently forward until you feel a stretch across the chest. Hold.
setup: Forearms flat on the frame, elbows at roughly 90° and shoulder height.
tempo: Hold 25–30 seconds, 2 rounds.
breathing: Breathe out and let the chest open a little further.
form_cues: Lead with the chest, not the chin.
Ribs down so the stretch stays in the chest rather than the lower back.
Vary the elbow height to catch different fibres.
why: The direct counter to a pressing session and to a day at a keyboard; a short chest lets the shoulder sit forward, which is where most bench-press shoulder pain begins.
common_mistakes: Pushing so far it pinches at the front of the shoulder.
Arching the lower back to lean further instead of opening the chest.

name: Wall Calf Stretch
instructions: Put your hands on a wall, step one foot well back with the leg straight and the heel down. Push the hips forward until you feel the stretch in the upper calf. Then bend that back knee slightly to move the stretch lower toward the Achilles. Hold each, then swap.
setup: Hands on the wall, back leg straight, back heel flat on the floor, toes pointing forward.
tempo: Hold 25 seconds straight-legged, then 25 with the knee bent.
breathing: Slow and steady.
form_cues: The back heel must stay down — lifting it removes the stretch entirely.
Back toes point straight at the wall, not turned out.
Do both versions: straight leg for the gastroc, bent knee for the soleus.
why: Ankle range is the most common hidden limit on squat depth. Two minutes here does more for a shallow squat than any amount of cueing.
common_mistakes: Letting the heel come up to get a bigger-feeling stretch.
Skipping the bent-knee version, which is the one that affects deep squatting.

name: Seated Spinal Twist
instructions: Sit with your legs out in front. Cross one foot over the opposite thigh, then rotate your torso toward the bent knee, using your arm against the knee as a gentle lever. Sit tall. Hold, then swap.
setup: Seated tall, one leg straight, the other foot planted across it.
tempo: Hold 25–30 seconds per side.
breathing: Inhale to grow tall, exhale to rotate a little further.
form_cues: Lengthen the spine BEFORE you rotate — twisting a slumped spine achieves nothing.
Rotate from the mid-back rather than yanking with the arm.
Keep both sit bones on the floor.
why: Restores rotation to a mid-back that heavy bracing tends to lock down, and it pairs naturally with the open-book drill from the warm-up.
common_mistakes: Cranking with the arm so the force goes into the lower back.
Slumping, which loses the rotation before it starts.

name: Figure-Four Glute Stretch
instructions: Lie on your back and cross one ankle over the opposite knee to make a figure four. Reach through and pull the bottom thigh toward your chest until you feel the stretch in the crossed glute. Hold, then swap.
setup: On your back, head down, one ankle resting on the opposite thigh just above the knee.
tempo: Hold 30 seconds per side.
breathing: Slow; let the hip release on each exhale.
form_cues: Keep the head and shoulders on the floor rather than curling up to reach.
Push the crossed knee gently away to deepen it.
Stop if you feel pinching at the front of the hip.
why: The most accessible glute stretch there is — everything happens lying down, so a tight or cranky hip has nowhere to cheat to.
common_mistakes: Lifting the head and shoulders, which turns it into an abdominal effort.
Pulling into pain rather than to a firm, tolerable stretch.
